text: Essential hypertension (EH) is still a global health problem. In 2025, it was estimated that 1.56 billion people globally would have EH [ 1 ]. Those populations with EH have a higher risk of coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and heart failure [ 2 ]. Recently, genetic polymorphism of Vitamin D receptor (VDR) has been linked to EH development in 30–50% cases [ 3 ]. Beyond essential hypertension (EH), VDR gene polymorphisms have also been linked to other common diseases such as osteoporosis [ 4 ], type 2 diabetes mellitus [ 5 ], and various autoimmune conditions, including multiple sclerosis [ 6 ] and systemic lupus erythematosus [ 7 ]. BsmI, FokI, ApaI, and TaqI polymorphisms have demonstrated varying degrees of association with these diseases due to their influence on vitamin D metabolism, immune modulation, and cellular differentiation [ 8 ]. However, the specific role of VDR polymorphisms in EH has not been fully elucidated, which justifies our focused analysis on EH in this study. Additionally, in cardiovascular metabolism, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25 [OH]2 D) binds to the VDR, a transcription factor in the aortic endothelium, and smooth muscle vascular cells to exercise its biological effects on myocardiocytes [ 9 – 11 ].
source_label: Association between vitamin D receptor gene polymorphism and essential hypertension: An updated systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression
